claims.claim: Operations management is the business function that plans, organizes, coordinates, and controls the resources needed to produce a company's goods and services; OpenStax's Introduction to Business frames managing the conversion process as the role of operations management, and this lesson attributes the working definition to OpenStax.
Production is the creation of products and services; production turns inputs such as natural resources, raw materials, human resources, and capital into outputs, which are products and services.

Operations management is also described as the administration of business practices to maximize efficiency, with the organization converting inputs such as materials, labor, and technology into outputs in an efficient manner; functions include quality control and delivery management.

Customer satisfaction is an important goal of effective production and operations, and a focus on quality is a central component of effective operations management; production planning lets the firm consider the competitive environment and its own strategic goals to find the best production methods.

Production methods: job production makes one item at a time to a customer's order (OpenStax's job shop produces goods in response to customer orders); batch production makes products in specified groups or amounts; flow/continuous production, synonymous with mass production, runs high volumes of standardized products continuously using automation or assembly lines.

Quality goods and services meet customer expectations by providing reliable performance, and from the manufacturer's point of view quality is the degree to which the product conforms to a set of predetermined standards.

Quality control involves creating quality standards, producing goods that meet them, and measuring finished goods and services against them; quality assurance is the systematic or planned actions necessary to offer sufficient reliability so that a product or service will meet its specified requirements.
Productivity is expressed as a ratio of output to input, i.e. output per unit of input, typically over a period of time.

The lesson's framing of operations versus strategy (execution versus direction) and its honest framing that operations is where plans become products are this lesson's synthesis: strategy sets direction while operations converts inputs into outputs day to day, and OpenStax grounds the link by tying production planning to the firm's strategic goals.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether quality control and quality assurance are the same activity
positions: The two terms are often used interchangeably in casual business talk.
OpenStax describes quality control as creating quality standards, producing goods that meet them, and measuring finished goods and services against them — an output-checking activity.
CFI defines quality assurance as the systematic or planned actions necessary to give sufficient reliability that a product or service will meet its requirements — a process-building activity.
The lesson names both simply and keeps them apart: quality control checks the output; quality assurance builds quality into the process.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches quality control and quality assurance as two named, distinct activities, following OpenStax for quality control and CFI for quality assurance, with the simple distinction of checking output versus preventing defects.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which naming scheme to use for production methods
positions: OpenStax frames the territory as three production types: mass production, mass customization, and customization, with customization delivered by job shops.

A common business-literacy naming, corroborated by CFI (mass production synonymous with continuous flow production) and Wikipedia (the job/batch/flow grouping), uses job production, batch production, and flow production.
The lesson adopts the job, batch, and flow naming as its chosen framing and notes that OpenStax frames the same territory as a customization-to-mass-production continuum.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names job, batch, and flow production, each with one line and when it fits, and records the OpenStax continuum so readers who meet either naming are not confused.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether efficiency and productivity mean the same thing
positions: The words are used interchangeably in everyday language.
CFI frames operations management as maximizing efficiency, and OpenStax connects routing and scheduling to productivity gains, treating both as ways to get more from the same resources.
Wikipedia defines productivity as output per unit of input.
The lesson states both simply at general-literacy level: efficiency is doing more with the same resources (cutting waste), productivity is output per unit of input, with no formulas.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents efficiency and productivity as related general ideas about doing more with the same resources, without formula depth, per the literacy level.
